title: Overview of Popular LLMs
learning_objective: Students will identify the four major LLM families, compare their strengths through live side-by-side use of their consumer apps, and make informed model selection decisions based on task, cost, and privacy requirements.
description_for_ai: This topic covers the four main LLM families: GPT (OpenAI) — best for code and general tasks; Claude (Anthropic) — best for long documents and writing, 200K token context window, Constitutional AI safety approach; Gemini (Google) — best for very long context (1M tokens) and multimodal tasks, free tier available; LLaMA (Meta) — open source, runs locally, best for privacy-sensitive applications and custom fine-tuning. Students paste the same prompt into ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini's web apps side by side and compare tone, style, and quality directly — no API calls or code yet, that begins in Topic 3. The topic also introduces the three ways people access these models (web chat, mobile app, and developer API) and walks through Nigerian business scenarios (a fintech support bot, a bank's loan-agreement summariser, a hospital records assistant) to practise picking the right model family for a given constraint.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming the most expensive or newest model is always best — the right choice depends on the task, not just capability. Not considering that a model requiring sensitive data to leave company servers may be unsuitable regardless of quality (relevant under NDPA 2023). Judging a model from a single prompt instead of testing several representative examples. Confusing "which model is accessible via a free web app" with "which model is cheapest to run at scale via API" — these are different questions.

title: Accessing LLMs via API
learning_objective: Students will set up API keys securely, make structured API calls with system and user messages, read the full response object, build multi-turn conversations, handle API errors with retry logic, and stream responses.
description_for_ai: This topic covers the full API access workflow. Students learn: secure API key management using `.env` files and `python-dotenv` (never hardcode keys — GitHub bots steal exposed keys within seconds); the anatomy of an API request — model, messages array (system/user/assistant roles), temperature, max_tokens; reading the response object — text at `response.choices[0].message.content`, token usage at `response.usage`, finish reason at `response.choices[0].finish_reason` (stop=natural end, length=cut off, content_filter=blocked); building multi-turn conversations by manually maintaining the messages array (LLMs have no memory — you must pass full history every call); error handling with try/except for AuthenticationError, RateLimitError, APIError with exponential backoff; streaming responses using `stream=True` and iterating over chunks. Nigerian business context used throughout.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Not including conversation history in follow-up calls — the model has no memory, each call starts fresh. Not setting `max_tokens` — responses can be very long and expensive without a cap. Not checking `finish_reason` — if it says "length", the response was cut off and max_tokens needs increasing. Using Python's `and`/`or` instead of catching specific exception types. Forgetting `flush=True` when streaming — output may not appear in real time without it.
example_code_for_ai:
# We import the tools we need, load our API key, and create the client

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

# This reads your .env file and loads the API key into memory
load_dotenv()

# This creates the client we will use to talk to the model
# The API key comes from your .env file — never hardcode it here
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))

# The system message tells the model who it is and how to behave
# It shapes every response in the conversation

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o-mini",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "system",   # This sets the model's role — it reads this before answering
            "content": "You are a business advisor specialising in Nigerian startups. Always give practical, Nigeria-specific advice using Naira amounts and local examples."
        },
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": "What are the top three industries driving economic growth in Nigeria right now?"
        }
    ],
    temperature=0.7,
    max_tokens=300
)

print(response.choices[0].message.content)

print("Prompt tokens:    ", response.usage.prompt_tokens)
print("Completion tokens:", response.usage.completion_tokens)
print("Total tokens:     ", response.usage.total_tokens)
print("Finish reason:    ", response.choices[0].finish_reason)   # 'length' = cut off, raise max_tokens

title: Introduction to Prompt Engineering
learning_objective: Students will apply zero-shot, one-shot, few-shot, role, and chain-of-thought prompting techniques, control output format for application development, and build a simple prompt chain.
description_for_ai: This topic teaches core prompt engineering techniques. Zero-shot: task without examples — works for common well-defined tasks. Few-shot: include 1–5 examples to show exact format or style — use for domain-specific tasks or when consistency matters. Role prompting: assign a persona in the system message ("You are a Nigerian tax lawyer who...") — dramatically changes tone, vocabulary, and cultural relevance. Chain-of-thought: add "Think through this step by step" — improves accuracy on multi-step reasoning and maths problems. Output format control: always specify format for production code — JSON output, numbered lists, strict bullet formats. Prompt chaining: break complex tasks into sequential simple prompts, each using the output of the previous. Nigerian examples: complaint classification, English-to-Pidgin translation, Lagos trader profit/loss calculation, CV screening for Nigerian tech companies.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Using zero-shot for domain-specific Nigerian tasks — few-shot with local examples dramatically improves results. Not specifying output format — leads to inconsistent outputs that cannot be parsed by application code. Putting multiple unrelated tasks in one prompt — chain them instead. Not testing prompts with varied inputs — a prompt that works once may fail 30% of the time. Writing system messages that are too vague — every unstated rule is filled in by the model's defaults.
example_code_for_ai:
# In Topic 3 we wrote out the full API call every time.
# Now we use a helper function called ask() to keep each cell short
# and focused on the prompt technique — not the API mechanics.

import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()
client = OpenAI(api_key=os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY"))

def ask(prompt, system=None, temperature=0.7, max_tokens=400):
    """Send a prompt to GPT-4o-mini and return the text response."""
    messages = []
    if system:
        messages.append({"role": "system", "content": system})
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": prompt})
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=messages,
        temperature=temperature,
        max_tokens=max_tokens
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content

# Now we include examples to show the model exactly what we want.
# This is especially useful for domain-specific or locally relevant tasks.

# Example 1 — complaint classification with examples
print("Few-shot complaint classification:")
print(ask(
    """Classify customer complaints into: Billing, Delivery, or Product Quality.
Return only the category — no explanation.

Complaint: I was charged twice for the same order.
Category: Billing

Complaint: My package never arrived after 2 weeks.
Category: Delivery

Complaint: The customer service agent was very rude to me.
Category:""",
    temperature=0
))

title: Structured Outputs & Validation
learning_objective: Define a Pydantic model that serves as both the JSON Schema sent to the API and the validator for the reply, extract structured data with response_format, enforce a business rule with a field_validator, and write a retry loop that feeds validation errors back to the model.
description_for_ai: Chat replies in prose come back in different shapes for the same meaning ('Severity: P2' versus 'classified as P2 - High'), so code that splits or regex-parses them breaks; downstream code needs data, not prose. A JSON Schema describes the exact shape wanted: a type and properties per field, enum for a fixed set of allowed values, and required for mandatory fields. Structured output mode passes that schema to the API and constrains the reply to match it, which is stronger than asking for JSON in the prompt. In Python, one Pydantic BaseModel does two jobs: its schema is what the API receives, and the class validates the reply. client.chat.completions.parse(model=..., messages=..., response_format=IncidentExtract) returns response.choices[0].message.parsed as an IncidentExtract instance, not a dict or a string. Literal['P1', 'P2', 'P3', 'P4'] restricts a field to fixed values; Optional[str] = None lets a field be absent, and the system prompt must say that null is acceptable, otherwise a required field pushes the model to invent a value. A @field_validator (with @classmethod) enforces business rules the type system cannot express, such as customers_affected >= 0, by raising ValueError, and Pydantic raises a ValidationError that names the failed field and rule. Structured output mode guarantees the shape of the reply, not that its values are correct. A retry loop catches ValidationError, appends the error to the messages as a correction request, and tries again up to a fixed cap (3 attempts), then raises RuntimeError so a human looks at it; every failed attempt is logged. The running example is a synthetic NOC incident report (NOC-INC-2026-0417) extracted into incident_id, severity, affected_link, customers_affected and root_cause.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Assuming structured output mode guarantees correct values; it guarantees shape only, so a valid severity such as 'P3' can still be the wrong one for the report. Wrapping only response.choices[0].message.parsed in try/except; validation runs inside the .parse() call, so the whole call must sit inside the try block. Making a field required when the source may not state it, which pushes the model to invent a value; use Optional[str] = None and tell the model null is acceptable. Retrying without a cap, or without feeding the ValidationError back to the model, or swallowing it with a bare except/pass that hides which field failed. Forgetting @classmethod under @field_validator, or using Pydantic v1 names (@validator, .json()) instead of field_validator and model_dump_json. Passing a dict or a string instead of the model class as response_format.
example_code_for_ai:
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator
from typing import Literal, Optional

class IncidentExtract(BaseModel):
    incident_id: str
    severity: Literal["P1", "P2", "P3", "P4"]
    affected_link: str
    customers_affected: int
    root_cause: Optional[str] = None  # None if the report does not state a cause

    @field_validator("customers_affected")
    @classmethod
    def must_be_non_negative(cls, v):
        if v < 0:
            raise ValueError("customers_affected cannot be negative")
        return v

response = client.chat.completions.parse(
    model=MODEL_NAME,
    messages=[
        {"role": "system", "content": "Extract incident details from the NOC report below. "
                                      "If the report does not state a root cause, leave root_cause as null rather than guessing."},
        {"role": "user", "content": INCIDENT_REPORT},
    ],
    response_format=IncidentExtract,
)
incident = response.choices[0].message.parsed   # an IncidentExtract instance, not a dict
print(incident.model_dump_json(indent=2))

title: Testing for Hallucination & Verification Habits
learning_objective: Compute an expected value by hand from a source document, compare a model's plain-text answer against it, and write pytest tests - including an offline pytest.raises test of a Pydantic validator that needs no API call - that would catch a wrong or invented answer.
description_for_ai: A model can be wrong while sounding right in two ways: it invents something the source never said, or it repeats a vague claim instead of computing the precise one. The running example is a NOC shift note with two timestamps, 02:14 (alarm raised) and 03:52 (service restored), and the summary line 'The outage lasted approximately two hours': the correct duration is 03:52 minus 02:14 = 98 minutes, while 120 is the rounded summary claim. Neither check needs a schema: a plain client.chat.completions.create() call returns a string, and re.search(r'\d+', text) pulls the number out to compare with the answer key. The answer key (KNOWN_DURATION_MINUTES = 98) is computed by hand from the source before any test runs, never by asking the model. When these exact checks were run live, the course model answered 98 on 6 of 6 runs, and answered 'Not mentioned' on 4 of 4 runs to a question the note never answers (who manufactured the failed amplifier); a passing result is a reason to keep the test, not delete it, because the model, prompt or gateway behind MODEL_NAME can change without warning. pytest collects functions named test_*; a plain assert passes silently or fails with both values shown (assert 120 == 98). pytest.raises(ValidationError) proves a validator rejects bad data, for example customers_affected=-3, with no API call. The live test and the offline validator test stay independent, so an API outage cannot hide or fail the validator result; run both with pytest test_extraction.py -v. Verification habits for AI-assisted code: read and be able to explain every suggested line, never accept a fix that swallows an exception (except: pass) to remove an error message, and run the test suite after every change.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Asking the model for the expected value used in the test, which lets the model grade itself. Testing only the shape of a result (correct type, valid enum value) and treating a valid shape as a correct answer. Deleting or skipping a test because the model currently passes it. Sharing one setup between the live-API test and the offline validator test, so an outage fails or masks both. Naming a test function without the test_ prefix so pytest collects nothing, or using pytest.raises without import pytest. Parsing the model's reply with int(text) or a digit regex when it answers in words ('ninety-eight'), which raises ValueError.
example_code_for_ai:
import re
import pytest
from pydantic import ValidationError

KNOWN_DURATION_MINUTES = 98  # 03:52 - 02:14, computed by hand from the shift note

def extract_minutes(text: str) -> int:
    match = re.search(r"\d+", text)
    if not match:
        raise ValueError(f"No number found in model reply: {text!r}")
    return int(match.group())

def test_duration_not_copied_from_summary():
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=MODEL_NAME,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Based on the shift note below, how long did the outage last, "
                                              "in minutes? Reply with just the number.\n\n" + SHIFT_NOTE}],
    )
    assert extract_minutes(response.choices[0].message.content) == KNOWN_DURATION_MINUTES

def test_negative_customers_rejected():   # offline: no API call
    with pytest.raises(ValidationError):
        IncidentExtract(incident_id="NOC-INC-2026-0417", severity="P2", affected_link="KU-HUB1-GW3",
                        customers_affected=-3, root_cause="unknown")

title: Git for the Shared Repo
learning_objective: Record work with git init, status, add, commit and log, isolate changes on feature branches and resolve merge conflicts, and share work through a GitHub remote using push, pull, clone, fork and pull requests.
description_for_ai: Version control records every change, allows rollback and supports collaboration, answering what changed, who changed it and how to undo it. Git is the version-control tool that runs locally; GitHub is the cloud platform that hosts Git repositories - they are not the same thing. Git works across three areas: Working Directory (edit files), Staging Area (git add) and Repository (git commit); files are Untracked, Modified, Staged, Committed or Ignored, and the core cycle is edit, stage, commit. git config --global user.name and user.email set the identity on commits; git init creates the hidden .git folder once, in the project root; git status shows file states and should run before and after staging; git add <file> or git add . stages changes; git commit -m saves a snapshot with a verb-first message describing what changed; git log --oneline shows compact history; git diff and git diff --staged show line-level changes. .gitignore must exist before the first commit and list .env (API keys), node_modules/ and OS files; git rm --cached .env stops tracking a file that was already committed. Branches isolate work from main: git switch -c feature/name creates and switches, commits on a feature branch stay invisible on main, git merge (run from main) brings them in, and git branch -d deletes the merged branch. A merge conflict happens when two branches edit the same line; Git inserts <<<<<<< HEAD, ======= and >>>>>>> branchname markers, and the fix is to edit the file to the correct version, remove all three marker lines, then git add and git commit. Remotes: git remote add origin <url>; git push -u origin main on the first push to set upstream (plain git push afterwards); git pull each morning to fetch teammates' commits; git clone once to copy a repository to a new machine; a Personal Access Token instead of a GitHub password for authentication. Collaboration flow: fork, clone the fork, create a feature branch, commit (with Closes #N to close Issue N on merge), push, open a Pull Request with a verb-first title and a description of what it does and how to test it, review with Comment, Approve or Request Changes, and merge with the default merge commit. Professional rule: never commit directly to main - every change goes through a feature branch and a pull request.
common_mistakes_for_ai: Confusing Git (the local tool) with GitHub (the hosting website). Committing before a .gitignore exists, so .env with API keys enters the history. Writing uninformative commit messages such as 'changes' or 'fix' instead of a verb plus what changed. Running git restore without --staged, which permanently discards working-directory changes. Merging while not on main so the merge runs in the wrong direction, leaving <<<<<<< or >>>>>>> markers in a file after a conflict, or forgetting to git add and git commit after resolving it. Creating the GitHub repository with a README when the local repository already has commits, producing diverged histories on the first push, or omitting -u on the first push so later git push commands fail. Using a GitHub password instead of a Personal Access Token, or using git clone when the repository already exists locally instead of git pull. Opening a pull request with no description, against the wrong base branch, or bundling unrelated features, and not using Closes #N so the Issue stays open.
example_code_for_ai:
git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@example.com"
git init
# create .gitignore containing .env BEFORE the first commit
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Add incident extraction script"
git log --oneline
git switch -c feature/add-validation
git add .
git commit -m "Add customers_affected validator"
git switch main
git merge feature/add-validation
git branch -d feature/add-validation
git remote add origin https://github.com/<user>/<repo>.git
git push -u origin main
git pull
